say: You skip breakfast, call it intermittent fasting, and then eat a family pizza at noon because the window is open.
Your body was built to go hours without food, but a long gap between meals isn't a magic fat-burning switch.
In one trial, people ate only from noon to eight in the evening, with no calorie limit, and after twelve weeks, they lost about the same weight as people eating three meals a day.
In a year-long trial, both groups had the same calorie limits, and adding an eight-hour eating window made no clear difference to their weight.
Across ninety-nine trials, fasting beat eating freely, but against ordinary dieting, it was mostly a tie.
The clock isn't magic. It's just one way to eat less.
So if an eating window helps you snack less, use it, and if it makes you raid the fridge at midnight, eat three proper meals instead.
Don't fast if you're pregnant or breastfeeding, have diabetes, or have ever had an eating disorder, and if you take medication, tell your doctor before you change how you eat.
Let's get you back to factory settings.

lowe2020: Lowe DA et al. Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med 2020;180(11): 12 weeks, 116 participants; the time-restricted group was "instructed to eat ad libitum from 12:00 pm until 8:00 pm and completely abstain from caloric intake from 8:00 pm until 12:00 pm the following day"; the comparison group "was instructed to eat 3 structured meals per day"; between groups -0.26 kg (95% CI -1.30 to 0.78; P = .63); "There were no differences in estimated energy intake between groups."; "Time-restricted eating, in the absence of other interventions, is not more effective in weight loss than eating throughout the day."
liu2022: Liu D et al. Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss. N Engl J Med 2022;386(16):1495 to 1504: 139 patients with obesity; "For 12 months, all the participants were instructed to follow a calorie-restricted diet that consisted of 1500 to 1800 kcal per day for men and 1200 to 1500 kcal per day for women."; "time-restricted eating (eating only between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.)"; "Changes in weight were not significantly different in the two groups at the 12-month assessment (net difference, -1.8 kg; 95% CI, -4.0 to 0.4; P = 0.11)."; "Among patients with obesity, a regimen of time-restricted eating was not more beneficial with regard to reduction in body weight, body fat, or metabolic risk factors than daily calorie restriction."
bmj2025: Semnani-Azad Z et al. Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials. BMJ 2025;389:e082007 (abstract rebuilt from the OpenAlex word index): "99 randomised clinical trials involving 6582 adults of varying health conditions (720 healthy, 5862 existing health conditions) were identified."; "All intermittent fasting diet strategies reduced body weight when compared with ad-libitum diet."; against continuous energy restriction, only alternate day fasting showed a benefit (mean -1.29 kg, 95% CI -1.99 to -0.59, moderate certainty)
cochrane2026: Garegnani L et al. Intermittent fasting for adults with overweight or obesity. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2026, Issue 2, CD015610 (abstract rebuilt from the OpenAlex word index): "We included 22 RCTs with 1995 participants."; "Compared to regular dietary advice, intermittent fasting may result in little difference in percentage weight loss from baseline (MD -0.33, CI -0.92 to 0.26; 21 studies, 1430 participants; low-certainty evidence"; "These findings focused on short-term effects (up to 12 months), limiting the applicability of this review."
nhslondon: NHS London (MyHealth London), Intermittent fasting (filed under which-diet-is-right-for-me in the page URL; no review date shown): "People with a history of eating disorders like anorexia and bulimia, and pregnant or breastfeeding women should not attempt intermittent fasting."; "Never attempt to delay or skip meals if you're pregnant, have had or are prone to eating disorders, or have diabetes."; "If you are on medication, you should always inform your healthcare team at your GP practice if you are changing your diet plan."
